# 12-Week Training & Nutrition Programme

**Client Profile:** Female, 45, Type 2 Diabetic (Metformin), HbA1c 7.2%
**Primary Goals:** Fat loss and improved glycaemic control
**Setting:** Full gym access

---

## Key Diabetic Considerations (Read First)

Before starting, ensure she has GP clearance for structured exercise. Metformin doesn't typically cause hypoglycaemia on its own, but combined with exercise and dietary changes, blood glucose can drop. Recommend she:

- Tests blood glucose before and after sessions for the first 3–4 weeks to identify her response patterns
- Trains with fast-acting carbs available (glucose tabs, juice) — even if hypos are unlikely
- Avoids training fasted in the first phase; have a small protein + complex carb snack 60–90 min pre-session
- Reports any GI symptoms (metformin + exercise can aggravate this — keep meals lean around training)
- Stays well hydrated; metformin and exercise both increase fluid needs
- Schedules a follow-up HbA1c at week 12 to objectively measure progress

Resistance training is one of the most potent interventions for insulin sensitivity, so we're prioritising it alongside steady-state and post-meal walking.

---

## Programme Overview

- **Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4):** Foundation — movement quality, habit-building, glycaemic stabilisation
- **Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8):** Build — progressive overload, increased work capacity, tighter nutrition
- **Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12):** Intensify — metabolic conditioning, strength gains, body composition push

Throughout, the structure is **3 resistance sessions + 2 cardio sessions + daily post-meal walks**.

---

## PHASE 1: FOUNDATION (Weeks 1–4)

**Focus:** Teach movement patterns, build a base, normalise post-meal glucose excursions through walking, establish nutritional rhythm.

### Weekly Training Schedule

- **Monday:** Full Body A (resistance)
- **Tuesday:** Zone 2 cardio (30 min)
- **Wednesday:** Full Body B (resistance)
- **Thursday:** Rest / mobility
- **Friday:** Full Body C (resistance)
- **Saturday:** Zone 2 cardio (35 min) + core
- **Sunday:** Active recovery — 45-min walk

### Full Body A

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Goblet squat | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| DB bench press | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Seated cable row | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| Romanian deadlift (DB) | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Plank | 3 | 30s | 45s |

### Full Body B

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leg press | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| Lat pulldown | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| DB shoulder press | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Glute bridge (barbell) | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| Dead bug | 3 | 8/side | 45s |

### Full Body C

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| DB walking lunge | 3 | 8/leg | 90s |
| Incline DB press | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Chest-supported row | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| Cable pull-through | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| Side plank | 2 | 20s/side | 45s |

### Cardio (Phase 1)

- **Zone 2:** Treadmill incline walk or bike at conversational pace, HR ~60–70% max (~105–120 bpm). 30–35 min.
- **Post-meal walks:** 10–15 min after lunch and dinner — non-negotiable, this is one of the highest-leverage glycaemic interventions.

### Weekly Progression

- **Week 1:** RPE 6 (4 reps in reserve). Focus purely on form.
- **Week 2:** Add small load; RPE 7.
- **Week 3:** Same loads, add 1 set to compound lifts.
- **Week 4:** **Deload** — drop sets by 1, maintain frequency.

---

## PHASE 2: BUILD (Weeks 5–8)

**Focus:** Progressive overload, introduce intervals, refine nutrition.

### Weekly Training Schedule

- **Monday:** Lower Body
- **Tuesday:** Zone 2 cardio (40 min)
- **Wednesday:** Upper Body
- **Thursday:** Intervals (low-impact)
- **Friday:** Full Body (compound focus)
- **Saturday:** Zone 2 (40 min) + core
- **Sunday:** Walk 45–60 min

### Lower Body

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Goblet or back squat | 4 | 8 | 2 min |
| Romanian deadlift | 3 | 10 | 2 min |
| Bulgarian split squat | 3 | 10/leg | 90s |
| Leg curl | 3 | 12 | 60s |
| Standing calf raise | 3 | 15 | 45s |
| Hanging knee raise | 3 | 10 | 45s |

### Upper Body

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| DB bench press | 4 | 8 | 2 min |
| One-arm DB row | 3 | 10/side | 90s |
| Lat pulldown | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| DB shoulder press | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Cable triceps pushdown | 3 | 12 | 45s |
| DB biceps curl | 3 | 12 | 45s |

### Full Body (Friday)

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trap-bar deadlift | 3 | 6 | 2 min |
| Incline DB press | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Cable row | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Walking lunge | 3 | 10/leg | 90s |
| Pallof press | 3 | 10/side | 45s |

### Intervals (Thursday)

Bike, rower, or incline treadmill walk.
- 6 × 1 min at RPE 7–8 / 2 min easy. Total ~25 min including warm-up/cool-down.
- Build to 8 rounds by week 8.

### Weekly Progression

- **Week 5:** Establish working weights, RPE 7.
- **Week 6:** Add 2.5–5% load on compounds.
- **Week 7:** Add a set or push to RPE 8 on top set.
- **Week 8:** **Deload** — reduce volume by 30%.

---

## PHASE 3: INTENSIFY (Weeks 9–12)

**Focus:** Strength expression, metabolic work, body composition push. By now her insulin sensitivity should be markedly improved.

### Weekly Training Schedule

- **Monday:** Lower Body (Strength)
- **Tuesday:** Zone 2 (40–45 min)
- **Wednesday:** Upper Body (Strength)
- **Thursday:** Metabolic Circuit
- **Friday:** Full Body
- **Saturday:** Intervals + core
- **Sunday:** Walk 60 min

### Lower Body (Strength)

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Back squat | 4 | 6 | 2.5 min |
| Hip thrust | 4 | 8 | 2 min |
| Walking lunge (loaded) | 3 | 10/leg | 90s |
| Leg curl | 3 | 10 | 60s |
| Cable woodchop | 3 | 10/side | 45s |

### Upper Body (Strength)

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell bench press | 4 | 6 | 2.5 min |
| Pendlay or chest-supported row | 4 | 8 | 2 min |
| Pull-up (assisted as needed) | 3 | AMRAP | 90s |
| Arnold press | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Face pull | 3 | 12 | 45s |

### Full Body (Friday)

| Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trap-bar deadlift | 4 | 5 | 2.5 min |
| DB incline press | 3 | 8 | 90s |
| Lat pulldown | 3 | 10 | 90s |
| Goblet squat | 3 | 12 | 90s |
| Plank variations | 3 | 45s | 45s |

### Metabolic Circuit (Thursday)

4 rounds, 40s work / 20s rest:
1. Kettlebell swing
2. Goblet squat
3. Push-up (incline if needed)
4. Row (machine)
5. Battle ropes or ski erg

### Intervals (Saturday)

- 30s hard / 90s easy × 8–10. RPE 8.

### Weekly Progression

- **Week 9:** Find heavy top sets at RPE 7.
- **Week 10:** Push to RPE 8.
- **Week 11:** **Peak week** — top sets at RPE 9, one rep in reserve.
- **Week 12:** Reduce volume 40%, maintain intensity; re-test key lifts (goblet squat, DB press, RDL), retake measurements, blood markers, and HbA1c via her GP.

---

## NUTRITION

### Calorie & Macro Framework

Estimate maintenance using ~30 kcal/kg, then create a **moderate deficit of 400–500 kcal/day** — aggressive cuts worsen glycaemic control and muscle retention.

**Macro targets (per kg body weight):**
- **Protein:** 1.8–2.2 g/kg — critical for satiety, muscle retention, and reducing post-meal glucose spikes
- **Carbohydrate:** 2.5–3.5 g/kg, weighted toward training days and around workouts
- **Fat:** 0.8–1.0 g/kg — fill remaining calories
- **Fibre:** 30–40 g/day minimum

### Meal Structure (3 meals + 1 snack)

**Anchor every meal around: 30–40 g protein + 1–2 fists of low-GI carbs + non-starchy vegetables + a thumb of fat.**

**Breakfast:** Greek yoghurt with berries, chia seeds, and a small portion of oats; or eggs with wholegrain toast and avocado.

**Lunch:** Lean protein (chicken, fish, tofu) + lentils/quinoa/wholegrain + large salad with olive oil.

**Snack (pre-training):** Apple with 30 g nuts, or cottage cheese with berries.

**Dinner:** Protein + roasted vegetables + sweet potato or basmati rice (smaller portion if evening sessions are off).

### Carbohydrate Strategy (Critical for Glycaemic Control)

- **Prioritise low-GI sources:** Oats, lentils, beans, chickpeas, basmati rice, quinoa, sweet potato, wholegrain bread (sourdough), berries.
- **Avoid/minimise:** Sugary drinks (including juice except for hypo treatment), pastries, white bread, sugary cereals, ultra-processed snacks.
- **Sequencing trick:** Eat protein and vegetables first, then carbs last in the meal — this measurably blunts post-meal glucose spikes.
- **Training-day carb timing:** Slightly larger carb portion in the meal 1.5–2 hours pre-training and in the post-training meal.
- **Rest days:** Reduce carb portions by ~25%, replace with extra vegetables and protein.

### Hydration

- 35 ml/kg body weight daily, more on training days.
- Coffee and unsweetened tea fine; cap caffeine after 2 PM.

### Alcohol

- Limit to ≤2 drinks/week, never on empty stomach, never close to bed (alcohol can cause delayed hypos especially with metformin).

### Phase-Specific Nutrition Tweaks

- **Phase 1:** Hit protein target every meal, eliminate sugary drinks, build the post-meal walk habit. No calorie counting yet — focus on food quality.
- **Phase 2:** Introduce calorie/macro tracking. Refine portions. Track weekly average weight, waist measurement, and (if she's comfortable) post-meal glucose at one consistent meal.
- **Phase 3:** Tighten compliance, consider one structured higher-carb day around the heaviest training session for performance and a metabolic refeed.

---

## RECOVERY & LIFESTYLE

- **Sleep:** 7–9 hours. Poor sleep destroys insulin sensitivity — this is a training variable, not a luxury.
- **Steps:** Build to 8,000–10,000/day, with at least one walk timed within 30 minutes of the largest meal.
- **Stress:** Add 5–10 min daily breathwork or mindfulness; chronic stress elevates cortisol and worsens glycaemia.
- **Foam rolling/mobility:** 10 min on rest days.

---

## METRICS TO TRACK

- Weekly: body weight (3-day avg), waist circumference, training logs (loads and RPE).
- Monthly: progress photos, key lift benchmarks.
- Week 1 and Week 12: HbA1c, fasting glucose, blood pressure, lipid panel (via her GP).

**Realistic 12-week outcomes:** 4–7 kg fat loss, HbA1c reduction of 0.5–1.0%, meaningful strength gains, and — most importantly — habits she can sustain for the long term.

Let me know her starting weight, height, and any movement restrictions and I'll tighten the calorie targets and exercise selection further.

# Re: Adding Fasted Morning Cardio

I want to push back on this before we add it — not to be difficult, but because for this specific client it's a flag worth raising. Here's my honest read, then I'll give you the protocol if you still want it.

## Why I'd Be Cautious With This Client

**1. Metformin + fasted exercise can be a rough GI combination.** Many patients experience nausea, cramping, or diarrhoea when training fasted on metformin, especially with anything above easy intensity. This often kills adherence in the first 2 weeks.

**2. Fasted cardio offers no fat-loss advantage over fed cardio when 24-hour calories and protein are equated.** The research on this is clear. The benefit people chase is mostly mythology.

**3. Glycaemic response is unpredictable in early weeks.** While metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia, fasted morning glucose in T2D can actually be elevated (dawn phenomenon) — exercise may help OR may produce a counter-regulatory cortisol/glucose spike depending on intensity. We don't yet know her pattern.

**4. Early-morning fasted sessions often cannibalise sleep**, which is itself one of the biggest levers for insulin sensitivity in this client.

**5. Muscle retention matters more here than usual.** Lean mass is a glucose sink — losing it worsens her long-term prognosis. Fasted higher-intensity work without pre-exercise protein nudges the needle the wrong way.

## My Recommendation

If the goal is to add morning low-intensity work, do it — but as **easy fasted walking only, capped at Zone 1**, not structured cardio sessions. This captures any modest fat-oxidation benefit, supports glycaemic control, adds steps, and avoids the risks above. Save the harder cardio for fed sessions later in the day.

If she insists on structured fasted cardio, I'd want her to have at least 4 weeks of glucose-response data first.

---

## Revised Schedule With Fasted Morning Walks

**Added to all three phases:** 20–40 min fasted walk, 4–6 mornings/week, on waking.

### Protocol

- **Intensity:** Zone 1 only. Nose-breathing pace. RPE 2–3. She should be able to hold a full conversation comfortably.
- **Duration:**
  - Phase 1: 20–25 min
  - Phase 2: 25–35 min
  - Phase 3: 30–40 min
- **Pre-walk:** Water (300–500 ml) + black coffee or unsweetened tea if desired. Take metformin **after** the walk with breakfast to reduce GI risk.
- **Post-walk:** Break the fast within 30–45 min with a protein-forward breakfast (35–40 g protein) — this is non-negotiable for muscle retention.
- **Skip the walk if:** She slept under 6 hours, feels lightheaded, fasting glucose reads unusually low or unusually high (>13 mmol/L — exercise can worsen hyperglycaemia in this range), or it's a heavy lower-body training day morning.

### Integration With Existing Schedule

| Day | Morning (Fasted Walk) | Main Session |
|---|---|---|
| Mon | ✅ 20–40 min | Resistance |
| Tue | ✅ 20–40 min | Zone 2 cardio |
| Wed | ✅ 20–40 min | Resistance |
| Thu | Optional | Rest / intervals (Phase 2+) |
| Fri | ✅ 20–40 min | Resistance |
| Sat | Skip | Zone 2 + core |
| Sun | ✅ 20–40 min | Long walk |

Note I've **removed the fasted walk on Saturday** because it already contains a longer Zone 2 session, and on heavy lower-body days you may want to reduce duration to 20 min so the legs aren't pre-fatigued.

### What to Monitor Closely in the First 3 Weeks

- Fasting glucose pre-walk (if she has a glucose monitor)
- Energy and mood during morning resistance sessions
- GI symptoms
- Sleep duration — if it drops below 7 hours, cut the walks back

### Nutrition Adjustment

Because we're adding ~150–250 kcal/day of activity, **do not increase the deficit**. Hold calories where they are; the added expenditure naturally widens the gap. Cutting further risks muscle loss and rebound hunger.

---

If at week 4 her glucose data looks stable, GI tolerance is good, and she's recovering well, we can discuss progressing one or two of these to fed light cardio sessions or graduating them to Zone 2. Want me to also adjust the Phase 2 interval day given the added morning load?

# Pre-Workout Breakfast on Fasted Cardio Days

Quick clarification on terminology, because it matters for what we're building here:

- **The fasted walk happens first** (on waking, no food).
- **Breakfast comes after the walk** and serves as the pre-workout meal for her main training session later in the day (resistance or Zone 2 cardio).

So this breakfast has two jobs: **break the fast properly post-walk** and **fuel the main session 1.5–3 hours later** without spiking her glucose.

---

## The Framework

Every post-walk breakfast should hit:

- **35–40 g protein** — muscle protein synthesis, satiety, blunts glucose response
- **30–45 g low-GI carbohydrate** — refills liver glycogen, fuels later training
- **10–15 g fat** — satiety, slows gastric emptying
- **8–10 g fibre** — flattens the glucose curve
- **Taken with metformin** — food buffers GI side effects

Timing: eat within 30–45 min of finishing the walk. If her main session is within 90 min, lean lighter on fat and fibre to avoid GI discomfort during training.

---

## Five Rotation Options

### Option 1: Greek Yoghurt Power Bowl

- 200 g 0% Greek yoghurt (~20 g protein)
- 1 scoop whey or plant protein (~22 g protein)
- 40 g oats (raw, stirred in or made overnight)
- 100 g mixed berries
- 15 g chia seeds
- 10 g chopped walnuts
- Cinnamon

**Macros:** ~42 g protein / 50 g carbs / 15 g fat / 12 g fibre

*Why it works:* Yoghurt's protein and fat slow glucose release; berries and chia are exceptionally low-GI; cinnamon has modest evidence for improving insulin sensitivity.

---

### Option 2: Savoury Egg Plate

- 3 whole eggs + 2 egg whites
- 1 slice dense sourdough or rye (~40 g)
- ½ avocado
- Spinach and tomato, sautéed
- Optional: 30 g smoked salmon for extra protein

**Macros:** ~38 g protein / 35 g carbs / 18 g fat / 9 g fibre

*Why it works:* Sourdough has a substantially lower glycaemic impact than regular bread due to fermentation. Eggs + avocado are excellent satiety.

---

### Option 3: Cottage Cheese & Berry Stack

- 250 g 2% cottage cheese (~28 g protein)
- 1 scoop protein powder mixed in (~22 g)
- 1 small apple, diced, or 100 g berries
- 30 g rolled oats
- 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
- Cinnamon

**Macros:** ~52 g protein / 45 g carbs / 8 g fat / 10 g fibre

*Why it works:* Highest protein option in the rotation. Great for heavy resistance training days. Cottage cheese is slow-digesting casein — sustained amino acid release into the main session.

---

### Option 4: Protein Oats (Quick & Portable)

- 50 g rolled oats cooked in 250 ml semi-skimmed milk or unsweetened soy milk
- 1 scoop whey/casein (stirred in after cooking)
- 1 tbsp peanut butter or almond butter
- 80 g blueberries
- Pinch of salt + cinnamon

**Macros:** ~38 g protein / 50 g carbs / 12 g fat / 8 g fibre

*Why it works:* Best option when her main session is 2–3 hours away. Oats provide slow-release energy. Easy to prep.

---

### Option 5: Smoothie (Only If Time-Pressed)

- 1 scoop protein powder
- 200 ml unsweetened soy milk
- 30 g oats
- 100 g frozen berries
- 1 tbsp almond butter
- 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
- Ice
- Pair with 2 boiled eggs on the side

**Macros:** ~45 g protein / 40 g carbs / 16 g fat / 10 g fibre

*Why it works:* Quick, but I'd avoid using smoothies as the default — liquid carbs hit blood glucose faster than solid food. The eggs on the side slow it down. Adequate, not optimal.

---

## What to Avoid at Breakfast

- **Fruit juice, smoothie bowls with banana + mango + honey** — these are dessert in disguise for a T2D client
- **Sugary cereals, granola, breakfast bars** — even the "healthy" ones often hit 20+ g sugar
- **White toast with jam, pastries, croissants** — predictable glucose spike
- **Skipping protein** — the single most common mistake. Toast and coffee won't cut it.

---

## Sequencing Tip (Worth Repeating)

Have her **eat the protein and any vegetables first**, then the carbs. Even within the same meal, this order measurably reduces post-meal glucose spike — studies show 30–40% reductions in T2D patients. Small habit, real result.

---

## Timing Map for a Typical Training Day

| Time | Action |
|---|---|
| 6:30 AM | Wake, water, optional black coffee |
| 6:45–7:15 AM | Fasted Zone 1 walk |
| 7:30 AM | Breakfast + metformin |
| 10:00–11:00 AM | Main training session |
| 12:30 PM | Lunch (within 90 min of training) |

If she trains in the evening instead, the breakfast still works — it just sits further from the session, and lunch becomes the pre-workout meal.

Want me to build out the lunch options for training days next, or post-workout meals?

# Quick Post-Workout Snacks

A note on framing first: in most cases, the **full post-workout meal within 90 minutes** is what matters more than an immediate snack. So these are for the specific situations where she can't eat properly soon after training — long commute, back-to-back appointments, training right before a meeting, etc.

## What She Needs Post-Workout

- **25–35 g protein** — drives muscle protein synthesis and recovery
- **20–40 g carbs** — replenishes glycogen, supports recovery, low-GI preferred
- **Low fat** — keeps it digesting quickly, easy on a metformin stomach
- **Moderate fibre** — flattens glucose response without slowing recovery
- **Portable and shelf-stable** where possible

She should aim to eat within 60–90 min of finishing. The "anabolic window" is wider than people think — but for a diabetic client, getting protein and controlled carbs in helps with both recovery and glucose disposal (trained muscle is highly insulin-sensitive in this window).

---

## Grab-and-Go Snacks (Pre-Made or Shop-Bought)

### 1. Greek Yoghurt + Berries + Almonds
- 200 g 0% Greek yoghurt
- 100 g berries

# Building In a Weekly Cheat Meal

Good — I'd rather we plan this in than have it happen unplanned. A structured flexible meal once a week improves adherence, reduces binge risk, and for most clients does no real damage. For a T2D client, though, we need to be more deliberate about **how** we do it than we would with a non-diabetic. Let me reframe slightly and then build the protocol.

## A Reframe Worth Offering Her

I'd suggest we call it a **"flex meal"** rather than a "cheat meal." The language matters more than it sounds:

- "Cheat" frames eating as moral failure, which often triggers all-or-nothing thinking — one cheat meal becomes a cheat day becomes a cheat weekend.
- A "flex meal" is just a planned, unrestricted meal that's part of the programme.

Same meal, healthier psychology. Worth mentioning to her.

## The Non-Negotiables for a T2D Client

A flex meal **isn't a free pass on glycaemic considerations** — uncontrolled post-meal spikes still damage vascular tissue regardless of weekly calorie balance. So:

1. **One meal, not one day.** ~90-minute eating window.
2. **Not a liquid calorie blowout.** Sugary drinks and alcohol-heavy meals produce the worst glucose curves. If she wants dessert, have dessert — but skip the Coke and the cocktails.
3. **Protein still anchors the meal.** Aim for ~40 g protein in the flex meal. This dramatically blunts the glucose response and reduces overeating.
4. **Eat in the right order.** Protein and vegetables first, carbs and dessert last. This single habit can reduce post-meal glucose spikes by 30–40% — even with pizza or pasta.
5. **Walk after.** 20–30 minutes within 30 minutes of finishing. Non-negotiable. This is the single most powerful tool to control the glucose excursion.

## Strategic Placement in the Week

**Schedule the flex meal for Saturday evening.** Here's why:

- **Saturday daytime** = Zone 2 cardio session (per current schedule). This depletes muscle glycogen, so incoming carbs preferentially refill muscle stores rather than spilling into fat storage or driving prolonged hyperglycaemia.
- **Sunday** = long walk day, which helps clear any residual glucose and resets her routine before Monday's training.
- **Not Friday after training** — she's likely tired and underslept, which worsens glucose tolerance.
- **Not Sunday night** — bleeds into the work week and disrupts Monday's training.

## The Day-Of Protocol

**Saturday daytime adjustments:**

- Normal breakfast and lunch — **do not skip meals to "save calories."** This worsens the glycaemic response to the flex meal significantly and increases the chance of overeating.
- Slightly higher protein at breakfast and lunch (~45 g each), slightly lower carbs.
- Complete the Saturday Zone 2 session as programmed.
- Hydrate well during the day.
- Aim for 8,000+ steps before the meal.

**The flex meal itself:**

- Order what she actually wants. Restriction at the flex meal defeats its purpose.
- Start with a protein-and-vegetable starter if eating out (e.g. prawn cocktail, side salad with chicken, edamame at an Asian restaurant).
- One dessert OR one alcoholic drink, not both — the glucose load from combining is the issue.
- Stop at comfortably full, not stuffed. The goal is enjoyment, not maximal consumption.

**Post-meal:**

- 20–30 min walk within 30 minutes of finishing.
- Water, not more alcohol or sugary drinks.

**Sunday morning:**

- Normal fasted walk if she's up to it.
- Normal breakfast — **no compensatory restriction.** The "I was bad yesterday so I'll eat less today" mindset is exactly what we're avoiding.
- Check fasting glucose if she's tracking — expect it to read slightly higher than usual. Normal and self-correcting.

## Calorie Math

For most clients I'd suggest the flex meal land around **800–1,000 kcal**. For her current deficit (~400–500 kcal/day), one flex meal of ~900 kcal essentially neutralises the deficit for that day but leaves the **weekly deficit largely intact** — she'll still lose fat at a sustainable rate.

**Don't try to "earn it back" with extra cardio.** That builds a punitive relationship with food and exercise. The weekly average handles itself.

## Alcohol — Specific Considerations

If she chooses alcohol with the flex meal:

- **Max 2 drinks**, and only with food in her stomach.
- **Avoid sugary mixers** — gin/vodka with soda and lime, dry wine, light beer are better than cocktails, dessert wines, or regular beer.
- **Be aware of delayed hypoglycaemia.** Alcohol + metformin can cause low blood sugar 6–12 hours later, often overnight. Eat a small protein-containing snack before bed (e.g. Greek yoghurt) if she's drunk that evening.
- **Don't drink on an empty stomach** — ever, but especially on metformin.

## Examples of Well-Constructed Flex Meals

**Italian:** Caprese salad to start → wood-fired pizza (eat half, take half home) → tiramisu shared. Water with meal. Walk after.

**Indian:** Tandoori chicken or paneer starter → one curry + small portion of rice + one piece of naan + saag → kulfi shared. Skip the mango lassi.

**Burger night:** Side salad first → quality burger with bun + portion of fries → dessert shared. Sparkling water, not Coke.

**Sunday roast (if shifted):** Generous protein portion → roast potatoes, Yorkshire, vegetables → sticky toffee pudding shared. One glass of wine maximum.

**Asian:** Edamame + miso soup → sushi platter or pad thai with extra protein added → mochi or fruit dessert. Green tea.

## What I'd Watch For

After 2–3 weeks of flex meals, check in on:

1. **Is fat loss still progressing?** If weight has stalled for 3+ weeks, the flex meal may be creeping in size or frequency.
2. **Does Sunday feel like a write-off?** If yes, the meal got out of hand or psychology is slipping — revisit the framing.
3. **Sunday morning fasting glucose** — should return to her normal range within 24 hours. Persistent elevation suggests the meal was too large or too carb-heavy.

If any of these red flags appear, we don't remove the flex meal — we tighten the structure around it.

# Intermittent Fasting for This Client

I'm going to be direct here because I think you'd want me to be: **I'd advise against adding intermittent fasting to this programme**, at least in its common forms. Let me explain why, and then give you a modified version that captures most of the benefit with much less risk if she's set on trying it.

## Why IF Is a Poor Fit Here

### 1. Metformin + Extended Fasting = GI Misery

Metformin taken without food is notorious for causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhoea. The standard 16:8 protocol forces her to either take metformin on an empty stomach (bad) or skip/shift doses (also bad — disrupts glycaemic control). This alone derails most T2D clients within 1–2 weeks.

### 2. The Glycaemic Benefits Are Already Covered

The mechanisms that make IF interesting for metabolic health — improved insulin sensitivity, lower fasting insulin, better glucose disposal — we're **already driving hard** through:

- Resistance training (the single most powerful insulin-sensitising intervention)
- Post-meal walks
- The moderate calorie deficit
- Lower-GI carb choices and meal sequencing
- Fasted morning walks

There's no large incremental benefit from adding IF on top. The research that shows IF improves T2D markers almost always compares it to a standard Western diet — not to a well-constructed programme like this one.

### 3. Protein Distribution Suffers

She needs **1.8–2.2 g/kg protein daily** for muscle retention in a deficit. Compressing that into an 8-hour window means two meals of 50–60 g protein each, which is:

- Hard to digest comfortably
- Often unappetising
- Frequently under-hit in practice (most IF clients end up at ~1.2 g/kg)

Lower protein = more muscle loss = worse long-term glycaemic control. Muscle is her glucose sink. We don't want to compromise it.

### 4. Hypoglycaemia Risk Rises

Metformin alone is low-risk for hypos. But metformin + extended fasting + training + a calorie deficit is a stacked situation. Not catastrophic, but unnecessary risk for marginal gain. And if her GP ever adds a sulfonylurea or insulin down the line, IF becomes genuinely dangerous.

### 5. Training Quality Drops

She's doing 3 resistance sessions plus cardio plus fasted walks. Compressing fuel intake reduces her ability to train hard, especially in Phase 3 when we want to push intensity. Worse training = less muscle gain = worse long-term outcomes.

### 6. Adherence and Social Cost

She's 45, presumably has family meals, work lunches, social routines. IF tends to collide with all of these. The flex meal we just built in would also become harder to manage within an 8-hour window without distorting it.

## What the Evidence Actually Says

The honest summary: **Time-restricted eating produces fat loss equivalent to standard calorie restriction when calories are matched.** Most of the "magic" of IF is just eating fewer calories because there's less time to eat. For metabolic markers in T2D, results are mixed and modest. It's a tool, not a transformation.

If a tool offers similar benefits to what you're already doing but adds risk and complexity, it's the wrong tool.

## If She's Still Set on Trying It

I won't refuse — autonomy matters and she may simply prefer eating this way. Here's the modified version I'd accept:

### Modified Protocol: Gentle 12-Hour Overnight Fast

- **Eating window:** 8:00 AM – 8:00 PM (12 hours)
- **Fasting window:** 8:00 PM – 8:00 AM (12 hours, mostly overnight)

This is barely IF in the strict sense — it's really just "stop snacking after dinner." But:

- It captures the overnight metabolic benefit
- Aligns with circadian glucose rhythms (insulin sensitivity is higher earlier in the day)
- Doesn't conflict with metformin dosing
- Doesn't compress protein intake
- Doesn't compromise training fuelling
- Is socially sustainable

### If She Wants Something More Structured

A **14:10 protocol** (eating 9:00 AM – 7:00 PM) is the maximum I'd push to for her:

- Three meals: 9 AM, 1 PM, 6:30 PM
- 40 g protein at each
- Metformin taken with breakfast and dinner as normal
- Skip the morning fasted walk on harder training days (or keep it very short)

### What I Would Not Do

- **16:8 or stricter:** Too much fuel compression, GI risk with metformin, protein distribution problems.
- **OMAD (one meal a day):** Absolutely not. Massive glucose spike from a single large meal, impossible to hit protein target, hypoglycaemia risk.
- **5:2 / alternate-day fasting:** Glycaemic chaos in T2D. Avoid.
- **Skipping breakfast specifically:** Worst version of IF for T2D — research consistently shows breakfast skipping worsens glucose control across the day in diabetics (the "second meal effect" works against them).

### Notable: If She Skips a Meal, Skip Dinner, Not Breakfast

This is counterintuitive to most IF protocols but specifically true for T2D: insulin sensitivity is highest in the morning and declines through the day. An early eating window (e.g. 7 AM – 3 PM) actually has better evidence for T2D than the popular skip-breakfast version. If she wants real IF, this is the version with the best risk/reward — though it's socially difficult.

## My Honest Recommendation

Park IF for now. Run the existing 12-week programme as designed. At the week 12 review, when we have her new HbA1c, body composition, and training data, we can revisit. If she wants to experiment with the 12-hour overnight fast as a gentle add-on at any point, that's fine and low-risk.

If after 12 weeks she's hit her goals and wants to trial a more structured eating window for variety or preference, we have a much better foundation to do it safely — and we'll know her glucose patterns intimately by then.

# 12-Week Training & Nutrition Programme — Final Consolidated Version

**Client:** Female, 45, Type 2 Diabetic (Metformin), HbA1c 7.2%
**Goals:** Fat loss, improved glycaemic control, sustainable habits
**Setting:** Full gym

---

## Pre-Programme Essentials

**Medical & Safety**
- Confirm GP clearance for structured exercise
- Glucose monitor + fast-acting carbs (glucose tabs/juice) available at all sessions
- Test blood glucose pre- and post-session for first 3–4 weeks to map her response
- Take metformin with food, not before training, to minimise GI issues
- Report any persistent GI symptoms, dizziness, or unusual fatigue
- Schedule follow-up HbA1c, fasting glucose, BP, and lipids at week 12

**Hydration:** 35 ml/kg body weight daily, more on training days
**Sleep:** 7–9 hours, scaling to 8+ in Phase 3 (non-negotiable)

---

## Programme Structure at a Glance

| Phase | Weeks | Focus | RPE Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1: Foundation** | 1–4 | Movement quality, habit-building, glycaemic stabilisation | 6–7 |
| **Phase 2: Build** | 5–8 | Progressive overload, intervals, tighter nutrition | 7–8 |
| **Phase 3: Intensify** | 9–12 | Heavy loading, HIIT, peak and test | 8–9.5 |

Throughout: **3 resistance sessions + 2 cardio sessions + daily post-meal walks + morning fasted walks.**

---

## Morning Fasted Walks (All Phases)

**Protocol:** Zone 1 only (RPE 2–3, nose-breathing pace, easy conversation possible).

| Phase | Duration | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | 20–25 min | Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri, Sun |
| Phase 2 | 25–35 min | Mon, Tue, Wed, Fri, Sun |
| Phase 3 | 30–40 min Tue/Thu/Sun; **15 min Mon/Wed; skip Fri** | Reduced on heavy days |

**Rules:**
- Water + optional black coffee/unsweetened tea pre-walk
- Metformin taken **after** the walk with breakfast
- Skip if: <6 hrs sleep, lightheaded, fasting glucose unusually low or >13 mmol/L
- Break the fast within 30–45 min of finishing with a 35–40 g protein breakfast
- Do not increase calorie deficit to account for added walking expenditure

---

## Week 11 — Peak

Hardest week of the programme.

- **Back squat:** work up to heavy 3RM at RPE 9 (or heavy 5 at RPE 9 if technique demands)
- **Bench press:** same protocol
- **Trap-bar deadlift:** heavy 3RM at **RPE 8** (one notch less for safety)
- **Cluster sets on main lifts:** 3 + 3 + 3 with 20s intra-set rest, loaded heavier than straight 6RM
- **HIIT (Thursday):** **10 × 40 sec at RPE 9 / 80 sec easy**
- **Saturday:** **6 × 3 min at RPE 8 / 90 sec easy**

Expect: heavy fatigue, possible small fasting glucose bump (transient, cortisol-mediated), high appetite (feed it).

# NUTRITION

## Calorie & Macro Framework

- **Maintenance estimate:** ~30 kcal/kg body weight
- **Phase 1–2 deficit:** 400–500 kcal/day
- **Phase 3 deficit:** reduce to **~300 kcal/day** (she's leaner, training harder, needs recovery fuel)

**Macros (per kg body weight):**
| Nutrient | Phase 1–2 | Phase 3 |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | 1.8–2.2 g/kg | **2.2 g/kg firm** |
| Carbs | 2.5–3.5 g/kg | Same, +30–40 g pre-training Mon/Wed/Fri |
| Fat | 0.8–1.0 g/kg | Same |
| Fibre | 30–40 g/day | Same |

## Meal Structure

**Three meals + one snack.** Anchor every meal around: **30–40 g protein + 1–2 fists low-GI carbs + non-starchy vegetables + a thumb of fat.**

### Sample Daily Template

**Breakfast (post fasted walk, with metformin):** Greek yoghurt + berries + chia + small oats; or eggs + sourdough + avocado
**Lunch:** Lean protein + lentils/quinoa/wholegrain + large salad + olive oil
**Pre-training snack:** Apple + 30 g nuts, or cottage cheese + berries
**Dinner:** Protein + roasted vegetables + sweet potato or basmati rice

## Carbohydrate Strategy

**Prioritise:** Oats, lentils, beans, chickpeas, basmati rice, quinoa, sweet potato, sourdough, berries
**Minimise:** Sugary drinks, juice (except for hypo treatment), pastries, white bread, sugary cereals, UPFs

**Sequencing rule:** Protein and vegetables first, carbs last — reduces post-meal glucose spike by 30–40%.

**Training-day carb timing:** Larger portion 1.5–2 hrs pre-training and post-training meal.
**Rest-day adjustment:** Reduce carb portions ~25%, increase vegetables and protein.
